newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Last Korean M*A*S*H unit "inactivated".
newsitem.headline: Last Korean M*A*S*H unit "inactivated".

text.p: Tears flowed on Wednesday as the last of the U.S. Army's surgical field hospitals in Korea, which inspired the hit movie and television show M*A*S*H, was "inactivated".

Two stars from the long-running TV comedy series -- David Ogden Stiers, better known as Major Charles Winchester III, and Larry Linville, who played Major Frank Burns -- were on hand for the ceremony at a U.S military base south of Seoul.

The now-defunct 43rd Surgical Hospital (Mobile Army) was the prototype for M*A*S*H 4077, the fictional unit made famous in the book and later the movie and the television series that was watched by millions of people around the world.
Its camouflaged tents have long been folded and the hospital has found permanent quarters at Camp Humphreys, home to some of the 37,000 U.S. troops still stationed in South Korea.
Wednesday's "inactivation ceremony" marked the unit's transition to a new status as part of the Deployable Medical System, known as DEPMEDS. Three similar M*A*S*H units remain outside Korea.

M*A*S*H revolved around wisecracking army surgeons during the 1950-53 Korean War. The movie, directed by Robert Altman, broke new ground in comedy and starred Donald Southerland, Elliot Gould, Tom Skirit and Sally Kellerman.
The television show also starred Alan Alda as Hawkeye and Loretta Switt as "Hotlips".
Gary Burghoff played "Radar" O'Reilly in both.
The final episode of the most popular television series in U.S. history aired almost 15 years ago, but reruns are attracting a new generation of fans.
The real-life 43rd M*A*S*H was formed in 1933 and saw service in Algeria, India, Burma and Japan before arriving in Korea in 1950.
At one point it set up in Pyongyang, now the capital of communist North Korea, which was briefly captured by U.S.-led forces during the Korean War.
On Wednesday, Stiers was handed a long knife, in lieu of his scalpel, to slice a celebratory cake.
"We were a plastic representation of the real people and coming back in touch with reality is touching," said a tearful Linville.
The M*A*S*H theme song, played by an army brass band, rolled across the grassy fields of Camp Humphreys as the unit's flag was carefully folded.
Also in attendance was Larry Gelbart, the creator of the TV Series, who said he first visited Korea in 1950 with legendary comedian Bob Hope to boost the morale of U.S. troops.
But his show was never a hit with Koreans. It was dropped by the local U.S. armed forces network in the 1980s after complaints that some of the jokes were racially insensitive.

"The TV show portrayed exactly what it's like to be in M*A*S*H," said Sergeant Alex Price, who spent a year with the 43rd unit. "There's a feeling of awe. I've been to war and seen lots die. Times have changed and the equipment has changed, but the people are the same."
M*A*S*H has been dubbed into several foreign languages, with hilarious results.
"You should see Frank Burns in Japanese," said Linville.
"I've been stupid in about 50 languages," added Stiers.
